canonical_topic: China vs. US carbon emissions dispute
definition: A geopolitical disagreement over how global carbon caps should be allocated between high-population, rapidly industrializing countries and already-industrialized countries.
core_idea: China's fast build-out of coal power means it will likely overtake the US as the top carbon emitter; China favors per-capita emissions caps (which would let it keep building coal plants), while the US resists a framework where it retires plants only for China to add more polluting capacity.
key_points: China and the US are described as the two largest carbon polluters, with China poised to overtake the US as it builds more coal plants
China's large population makes a population-based (per-capita) cap structure favorable to it, since it would permit continued coal buildout
The US position is that it shouldn't bear the cost of shutting down less-polluting plants if that capacity is simply replaced by more-polluting Chinese plants
The author frames the underlying dispute as being about who ultimately pays a higher cost for power
relationships: Motivates the choice between carbon taxes and cap-and-trade as competing policy tools
